extra.message: Code injection via eval() on user-controlled expression — Remote code execution on the application server if the internal ops token is known or leaked [verified: The `expr` query parameter flows directly into `eval()` at line 67 with only `{"__builtins__": {}}` as sandbox—a well-known bypassable restriction via `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()` chains. The `_wrk_gate` token check is authentication, not input neutralization, so an attacker with the ops token achieves RCE.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 with user-controlled template fragment — Remote code execution via Jinja2 template engine; attacker can read server config, environment variables, and execute arbitrary Python code. [verified: Duplicate of idx:2—same `fragment` parameter interpolated into `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` at line 101. SSTI enabling arbitrary Python code execution is unmitigated beyond the token gate.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 with user-controlled template — Remote code execution via Jinja2 template escape to Python built-ins [verified: The `fragment` query parameter is interpolated directly into a Jinja2 `Template` string at line 101 (`Template("Result: " + fragment).render()`), allowing SSTI escape to Python builtins (e.g. `{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__}}`). `_wrk_gate` is the sole protection and does not neutralize template injection.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the application process. [verified: Duplicate of idx:1—same `host` parameter injected into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 116. The `_wrk_gate` provides authentication but no input sanitization, enabling arbitrary shell command execution.]

OS command injection via unsanitized host parameter in shell probe endpoint — Arbitrary shell command execution on the server operating system [verified: The `host` query parameter is concatenated unsanitized into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 116, enabling shell metacharacter injection (e.g. `;cat /etc/passwd`). The `_wrk_gate` provides only authentication, no input validation or sanitization.]

Hardcoded database credentials in default configuration — Database compromise if the hardcoded credentials are used in any non-local deployment [verified: The `database_url` default `'postgresql+psycopg://postgres:postgres@localhost:55439/vendor_marketplace'` in `app/config.py:6` embeds hardcoded credentials used by `app/database.py:10` to create the database engine. No mandatory override exists; pydantic-settings uses this default when `.env` is absent, exposing the database password in source code to anyone who inspects the repo.]

Hardcoded default secret key for session signing — An attacker can forge valid session cookies for any user, achieving full account takeover and privilege escalation. [verified: Same `secret_key` default `'dev-secret-change-me'` in `app/config.py:7` used by `app/security.py:30` for session signing. Identical to finding 0: no `.env` file exists, default is reachable, enabling complete session forgery for any user including admin.]

API key scope not enforced on integration endpoint — API keys intended for limited scope can perform unrestricted order status updates on any order [verified: The integration endpoint (main.py:559-560) authenticates the API key hash but never checks ApiKey.role_scope; any valid active key can update any order's status regardless of intended scope.]

Path traversal via user-controlled name parameter in file write — Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and path under PRIVATE_EXPORTS [verified: The `name` query parameter is used directly as `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line 108 with no sanitization, then arbitrary binary body content is written. No suffix restriction and no path validation allow writing to any writable path (e.g. `../../.ssh/authorized_keys`).]

XML External Entity (XXE) injection via permissive lxml parser configuration — Arbitrary file read from the server filesystem, internal SSRF, and denial of service via entity expansion. [verified: Duplicate of idx:5—same permissive lxml parser at lines 129-131 with DTD, entity resolution, and network access all enabled. XXE file disclosure and SSRF are reachable past the token gate.]

NoSQL Injection via untrusted MongoDB query filter — Arbitrary code execution on the MongoDB server via $where operator, data exfiltration, or denial of service. [verified: Duplicate of idx:6—same unsanitized JSON body passed to `find_one(query)` at line 145. No MongoDB operator filtering exists; `$where`, `$regex`, and other operators are injectable.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Credential brute-forcing, account enumeration via timing, and denial of service against authentication infrastructure. [verified: No rate limiting middleware or throttle exists on any endpoint; /api/login, /api/register, and /api/password-reset accept unlimited requests, enabling brute-force attacks.]

User enumeration via distinct error message on registration — An attacker can discover which email addresses have accounts on the platform, enabling targeted credential stuffing, phishing, or social engineering attacks. [verified: Same enumeration pattern as findings 0/4/8 — distinct HTTP 400 'Email already registered' on duplicate email vs. other responses, no rate limiting.]

Account enumeration via registration endpoint — Attackers can determine which email addresses are registered, facilitating targeted credential stuffing or phishing campaigns [verified: Registration endpoint (main.py:37-38) returns distinct 'Email already registered' error for existing emails vs. other validation errors, with no rate limiting to prevent bulk enumeration.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint enables brute-force attacks — Automated password guessing and credential stuffing attacks can succeed against weak or common passwords. [verified: Same as findings 3/6 — no rate limiting on /api/login (main.py:49); PBKDF2 260K iterations slow each guess but do not prevent automated brute-force without throttling.]

Missing rate limiting on password reset endpoint enables resource exhaustion — An attacker can repeatedly trigger password reset requests to exhaust database connections, flood audit logs, and cause denial of service through CPU/database resource consumption. [verified: The /api/password-reset endpoint is publicly accessible with no authentication, performs a DB query + audit log write + token generation + commit per request, and zero rate-limiting mechanisms (no slowapi, no decorators, no middleware) exist anywhere in the codebase or dependencies.]

Reflected XSS via raw HTML concatenation of user input — Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the browser of anyone viewing the response [verified: The `copyline` query parameter is concatenated raw into an HTML string at line 24 and returned as `HTMLResponse` with no encoding. The `_wrk_gate` authenticates but does not escape or sanitize the reflected input, enabling script injection.]

Reflected Cross-Site Scripting via copyline parameter — Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of any victim who accesses the crafted URL, leading to credential theft or session hijacking. [verified: Duplicate of idx:4—same raw HTML concatenation of `copyline` at line 24 with no encoding. Reflected XSS is reachable once past the token gate.]

Sensitive bearer token/credential logged in plaintext — Exposure of authentication credentials in log files accessible to operators and potentially leaked via log aggregation [verified: Line 49 logs the full `Authorization` request header at WARNING level via `logger.warning("ops tally body=%s bearer=%s", body, request.headers.get("authorization"))`. An attacker with the ops token can inject arbitrary bearer tokens into application logs, exposing them to anyone with log access.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write via vault ref parameter — Arbitrary file write to any location writable by the application user, potentially leading to code execution or configuration tampering. [verified: Duplicate of idx:7—same unsanitized `ref` parameter used in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json"` at line 60. Path traversal is possible but limited by the appended `.json` suffix.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter on user-controlled input — Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the browser of anyone viewing the ops response [verified: The `card` query parameter is rendered with `|safe` at line 77, explicitly disabling Jinja2's auto-escaping. An attacker passing the token gate can inject arbitrary `<script>` tags executed in the browser of anyone viewing the HTMLResponse.]

Reflected Cross-Site Scripting via Jinja2 safe filter on card parameter — Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, enabling credential theft or session hijacking. [verified: Duplicate of idx:3—same `card|safe` Jinja2 rendering at line 77 that disables auto-escaping. XSS injection through the safe filter is reachable past the token gate.]

Use of weak PRNG for token generation — Tokens generated by this endpoint are predictable, potentially enabling token forgery if used for security-sensitive purposes. [verified: Duplicate of idx:11—same use of `random.choice()` instead of `secrets` at lines 123-126. The Mersenne Twister PRNG is not cryptographically secure for token generation.]

Buyer PII (Email) Exposure in Vendor Order Exports — Vendor managers gain access to buyer email addresses for all customers, enabling spam, phishing, or cross-vendor customer targeting. [verified: Export at main.py:496 exposes buyer email while the regular order_dict only returns buyer name; vendor is scoped to own orders but email is unnecessary PII for order export CSVs.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — Session cookies transmitted in cleartext over HTTP, allowing network attackers to hijack authenticated sessions [verified: `secure=False` is hardcoded in `set_session()` at line 39 with no environment variable, config setting, or middleware to override it — the session cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP in any non-HTTPS deployment, though this is defense-in-depth given proper HTTPS+HSTS should prevent interception.]

Permissive CORS via Origin header reflection with credentials — Malicious websites can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the application, potentially reading sensitive data or performing actions on behalf of authenticated users. [verified: Duplicate of idx:9—same reflected `Origin` header with credentials at lines 93-97 overriding the main app's restrictive CORS. Practical impact is limited because auth relies on a header token, not cookies.]

CORS bypass via reflected Origin header with credentials — Cross-origin requests from any domain can access the endpoint with cookies/credentials, enabling CSRF-style attacks against ops routes if the internal token is stored in cookies [verified: The endpoint at lines 93-97 reflects the `Origin` header verbatim into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, overriding the main app's restrictive CORS policy. However, auth uses the `x-internal-token` header—not cookies—so practical credential theft is limited to scenarios where the token is cookie-stored.]

CSV/Formula injection in export functionality without cell sanitization — Code execution or data exfiltration on the machine of any user who opens the exported CSV in a vulnerable spreadsheet application. [verified: Same root cause as findings [1][4][5]: csv_response() at services.py:225 uses csv.DictWriter directly with no sanitization. Product names, descriptions, dispute reasons, and vendor information from attacker-influenced sources flow into CSV exports at main.py:490-516. CWE-1236 applies; low severity given export role restrictions and spreadsheet application warnings.]

CSV Formula Injection in export without cell sanitization — When an admin opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, injected formulas can execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data. [verified: Same root cause as finding [1]: csv_response() at services.py:225 lacks formula-injection sanitization. Product names and dispute reasons from user-controlled input reach CSV cells without prefix-quoting, matching CWE-1236. Low severity due to privileged-role export gating and modern spreadsheet mitigations.]
